title: U.S. House · Wyoming At-Large
area: The entire state of Wyoming, which has a single at-large U.S. House district.

context.text: This is an open seat: incumbent Harriet Hageman (R) is running for U.S. Senate rather than re-election to the House. Chuck Gray, Wyoming's current Secretary of State, won the Republican primary. Lisa Kinney, a former state senator, defeated Elena Del Real in the Democratic primary on August 18, 2026 with 74.6% of the vote.

summary.text: Chuck Gray is Wyoming's Secretary of State and a former three-term state representative, running as the Republican nominee for Wyoming's open at-large U.S. House seat. He took over his family's Casper radio business after college, served in the Wyoming House from 2017 to 2023, and was elected Secretary of State in 2022. In his announcement he said he was running to continue fighting for Wyoming's way of life and to advance President Trump's agenda.

background.text: Raised outside of Los Angeles, California, and spent summers with his father in Casper, Wyoming.
Earned a B.S. in economics from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania in 2012, according to the Secretary of State's biography.
Says he took over his family's radio business in Casper after graduating from college; Ballotpedia lists his career experience as radio executive and radio show host.

Served three terms in the Wyoming House of Representatives, District 57 (Natrona County), from 2017 to 2023; committees included Minerals, Business & Economic Development; Agriculture, State and Public Lands; Revenue; Judiciary; and Management Audit.
In the legislature he was lead sponsor of the ultrasound bill and of Wyoming's voter ID law, which was signed in 2021, according to his official biography.

Elected Wyoming's 24th Secretary of State in 2022 and took office in 2023; the office oversees elections, business entity registration and securities regulation, and he sits on the State Loan and Investment Board, the Board of Land Commissioners and the State Building Commission.
Announced his run for the U.S. House on December 29, 2025, after Rep. Harriet Hageman announced she would run for U.S. Senate.
Won the August 18, 2026 Republican primary in a ten-candidate field with 24.9% of the vote.

priorities.text: "I passed Wyoming's historic voter ID law to stop cheaters from trying to steal our elections. Election Integrity has been and will continue to be my top priority..."
"As a member of the legislature, I led the effort to cap property taxes... I go to work everyday to take power away from government and give it back to you."

positions.summary: Voted yes on HB0092, limiting the circumstances under which an abortion may be performed, contingent on the reversal of Roe v. Wade.
Voted yes on HB0116, which removed the state residency requirement for permitless concealed carry of a firearm.

stated.quote: PRO-LIFE & PRO-2ND AMENDMENT... both issues are about protecting the innocent from harm.

record.text: As a Wyoming state representative, led passage of a voter ID law requiring identification to vote, enacted in 2021.
Voted yes on HB0075 (requiring voters to present identification before voting in person), which passed the Wyoming House 51-9 on March 3, 2021.
Voted yes on HB0116 (removing the state residency requirement for permitless concealed carry of a firearm), which passed the Wyoming House 56-4 on March 17, 2021.
Voted yes on HB0092 (limiting the circumstances under which an abortion may be performed, effective if Roe v. Wade were overturned), which passed the Wyoming House 43-16 on March 1, 2022.

candidates.name: Lisa Kinney
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 18 Democratic primary with 74.6% of the vote

summary.text: Lisa Kinney is a Laramie attorney and former Wyoming state senator running as the Democratic nominee for Wyoming's open at-large U.S. House seat. She has worked as a librarian, lawyer, bar exam instructor and financial advisor, and served ten years in the state Senate, including two as minority floor leader. She says she is running on keeping public lands in public hands and on affordability.

background.text: Born and raised in Laramie, where she still lives; graduated from Laramie High School.
Earned an undergraduate degree from the University of Wyoming, a graduate degree (M.L.S.) from the University of Oregon in 1975, and a law degree from the University of Wyoming in 1986.

Describes owning Summit Bar Review, where she taught Wyoming and federal law to new lawyers preparing for the bar exam, and working as a partner at the law offices of Corthell & King and at the American Heritage Center.

Served as director of the Albany County Library, where she says she passed a bond issue for a new library, and later served as a compliance officer for the University of Wyoming, according to news coverage.
Worked for about 20 years as a financial advisor for VALIC/AIG/Corebridge; describes herself as a past president of the Laramie Area Chamber of Commerce and the author of four published books.

Served ten years in the Wyoming State Senate representing Laramie, rising to Senate Minority Floor Leader in her final term (Cowboy State Daily dates her service 1985 to 1994); she served on the Education and Judiciary Committees.
Defeated Elena Del Real in the August 18, 2026 Democratic primary with 74.6% of the vote.

priorities.text: "My priorities are to maintain our public lands, lower health care costs, and put more money in people's pockets through legislative changes."
"We must keep public lands in public hands... I will fight every attempt to sell off our public lands."

positions.summary: Says she would work to remove tariffs to lower costs for families.
positions.quote: I will work to remove tariffs, decrease the damaging provisions of the "Big Beautiful Bill," lower or delete income taxes and FICA.

positions.summary: Supports restoring ACA subsidies and working toward Medicare for All.
positions.quote: I am interested in pursuing universal healthcare by first bringing back the ACA subsidies to lower health insurance premiums right away and then working toward Medicare for all.

candidates.name: Jeff Haggit

summary.text: Jeff Haggit is a retired electrician and instrumentation technician from Mountain View, Wyoming, running as the Constitution Party candidate for Wyoming's open at-large U.S. House seat. He has served as state chair and is currently vice-chairman of the Constitution Party of Wyoming, and he ran for the same seat in 2020 and 2024.

background.text: Born in Midland, Michigan, and grew up in farm country; he has lived in Wyoming for about 50 years and in Mountain View for 22.
Graduated from Western Wyoming College in 1978.

Retired from the TATA trona processing facility in southwest Wyoming after almost 49 years as an electrician and instrumentation technician, according to his questionnaire answers; he also served as a trustee of the workers' Accident and Illness fund.

Has served as state chairman of the Constitution Party of Wyoming and currently describes himself as its vice-chairman; also a member of the United Way of Southwest Wyoming's Uinta Advisory Council and a 2016 graduate of the Uinta County Leadership Institute.
Ran for Wyoming's U.S. House seat as the Constitution Party candidate in 2020, receiving 7,905 votes (2.9%), and in 2024, receiving 5,362 votes (2.1%).

priorities.text: "My intention is to provide the citizens of Wyoming an opportunity to vote for someone who will not waver from their sworn duty to uphold Constitutional law, protect their rights, and work to restore the multitude of liberties robbed from them by both Republicans and Democrats..."

candidates.researchNotes: Has not completed Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey; no clear stance found on the guide's fixed issue list.

candidates.name: Shawn Johnson

summary.text: Shawn Johnson is a U.S. Army National Guard veteran, former Casper City Council member and attorney running as the Libertarian nominee for Wyoming's open at-large U.S. House seat. He served as a combat medic and a county jail deputy before holding local office and earning a law degree. He says he is running to restore constitutional limits on government and to give Wyoming an independent voice in Congress.

background.text: Wyoming native, born in Casper; spent his middle and high school years in the Denver area before moving back to Casper in 2007.
Served in the Army National Guard as a combat medic for 21 years (2000 to 2021), including a deployment to Iraq in 2003-2004.
Spent 13 years as a Natrona County Sheriff's Office jail deputy.
Earned an associate degree from Casper College (2016), a bachelor's degree from the University of Wyoming (2019), and a law degree from the Mitchell Hamline School of Law (2024).
Served two terms on the Casper City Council from 2014 to 2022, including one year as vice mayor in 2019.
Ran for the Wyoming House in 2020 and for the Natrona County Commission in 2022 as a Libertarian, according to Cowboy State Daily.

Now a practicing attorney, with a practice including family law, criminal defense and civil litigation; lives in Thermopolis. Nominated unanimously at the Libertarian Party of Wyoming convention on May 31, 2026.

priorities.text: "Wyoming deserves a representative who answers to Wyoming—not Washington, a political party, or the White House. I will not blindly follow party leadership."
"We need fiscal responsibility, less unnecessary government interference, and an economy where hard work can once again lead to prosperity."

candidates.researchNotes: Completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey but responses do not clearly state positions on the guide's fixed issue list.

researchNotes: Daniel Workman withdrew as an independent candidate and did not make the ballot. This is an open seat; no federal key votes or FEC House incumbency data apply. Lisa Kinney served ten years in the Wyoming Senate in the 1980s and 1990s (sources differ slightly on the exact years); individual floor roll-call votes from that era were not locatable within the research window (Wyoming's searchable digital legislative archive covers recent sessions reliably, and the pre-1995 scanned journals were not searched page-by-page here), so her record entry relies on her own campaign statements. No campaign websites were located for Haggit or Johnson; their biographies rely on Ballotpedia, WyoFile questionnaire answers and news coverage.
